title: Engineering voice agents: Latency, quality, and scale — Rishabh Bhargava, Together AI

summary:
Rishabh Bhargava from Together AI outlines why voice agents matter and the engineering challenges of building them at scale. Voice represents a natural interface—humans learn speech before reading—and billions of annual phone calls remain human-handled. The hard requirement is simultaneity: agents must be real-time (humans respond in ~300ms; users notice latency above 500ms and hang up above 1–2s), intelligent enough for complex workflows and tool calling, natural-sounding with correct accents, names, and emotions, and reliable across thousands of concurrent calls.

The dominant production architecture is a cascading pipeline: audio chunks stream into an orchestrator (e.g., Pipecat, LiveKit), then through STT, LLM, and TTS, with audio streamed back. The LLM consumes the majority of both latency and cost budgets, followed by TTS and then STT. Engine latency alone is insufficient—network latency between data centers matters. Co-locating all components in the same building drops network latency from ~75ms to ~5ms, a 30% reduction. Auto-scaling is tricky: scale-up must be aggressive, but scale-down requires care due to stateful long-lived connections.

An emerging alternative is pure speech-to-speech models (e.g., OpenAI real-time API, Nvidia Voice Chat), which preserve tone and emotion, enable full-duplex communication with back-channeling, and handle interruptions more naturally. However, these still struggle with instruction following and tool calling, limiting production use. For observability with speech-to-speech, a transcription model can run alongside to provide auditability of incoming and outgoing audio. Evals shift from text-based metrics to full-duplex conversation evals covering entire conversations, typically running on top of the base inference API. For production reliability, guardrails and classifier models can be added before or after the main LLM, though they add latency pressure. The thinker-talker pattern addresses complex workflows: a small LLM handles conversation flow and issues a single tool call to a larger model when needed, keeping the fast path fast. Fine-tuning smaller LLMs with use-case-specific data improves tool calling quality while staying within latency budgets.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Voice agents must solve latency, intelligence, naturalness, and reliability simultaneously — it is an 'and problem,' not a trade-off.
The LLM consumes the majority of both latency and cost budgets, followed by TTS, then STT.
Co-locating all models and the orchestrator in the same data center reduces network latency from ~75ms to ~5ms, a 30% reduction in an already optimized system.
Auto-scaling for voice agents requires aggressive scale-up but careful scale-down due to stateful long-lived connections that cannot be killed mid-conversation.
Pure speech-to-speech models preserve tone, emotion, and enable full-duplex back-channeling, but still struggle with instruction following and tool calling for production use.
The thinker-talker pattern uses a small LLM for conversation flow with a single tool call to a larger model for complex requests, keeping the fast path within latency budget.
With pure speech-to-speech models, a transcription model can run alongside to provide auditability, and evals shift to full-duplex conversation-level metrics on top of the base inference API.
Tool call structure accuracy should approach 100%; fine-tuning smaller LLMs with use-case data improves tool calling while staying within latency constraints.
Guardrails and classifiers add latency pressure; catching problematic outputs before TTS is critical since spoken responses cannot be taken back.
LLM TTFT target is 200–300ms, constraining models to 8–30B parameters; STT targets ~6% WER with P90 under 100ms; TTS real-time factor should be below 1.0.

sections.title: Introduction and agenda
sections.summary: Rishabh Bhargava introduces himself and Together AI, the AI native cloud platform for training and inference. He outlines the agenda: why voice matters, pipeline architecture, deep dive into components and trade-offs, and next-generation approaches.

sections.title: Why voice matters
sections.summary: Billions of annual phone calls are still human-handled. Voice is a natural new interface — humans learn to talk before reading — evidenced by ChatGPT advanced voice mode and people talking directly to Cursor and Claude Code.

sections.title: Why voice agents are hard
sections.summary: Four simultaneous requirements: real-time latency (300ms human cues, 500ms notice threshold, 1–2s hang-up threshold), sufficient intelligence for complex workflows and tool calling, natural-sounding speech with correct accents/names/emotions, and reliability at scale. All must be solved together.

sections.title: Pipeline architecture overview
sections.summary: The dominant cascading architecture: audio chunks stream into an orchestrator (Pipecat, LiveKit, or homegrown), then through STT to text, into an LLM that decides on tool calls and output, then into TTS producing audio chunks streamed back to the user.

sections.title: Speech-to-text component
sections.summary: STT is the ears of the agent. Key metrics: word error rate (~6% state-of-the-art) and time to complete transcript (P90 ~100ms on Together). Turn detection remains unsolved. Streaming-native architectures are evolving from batch Whisper (30s clips, requiring chunking) toward models with variable look-ahead (80ms–1s) and activation caching (e.g., Nvidia).

sections.title: LLM component
sections.summary: LLM is the brains. Streaming latency (TTFT) target is 200–300ms. This constrains model size to 8–30B parameters: larger models blow the latency budget, smaller models lack intelligence and tool calling capability needed for meaningful agents.

sections.title: Text-to-speech component
sections.summary: TTS is the voice of the agent. Key metrics: time to first audio and real-time factor (should be <1 to avoid buffering). Quality still requires subjective listening. Other capabilities: naturalness across voices, correct pronunciation of names/products, emotional control via tags, and language coverage.

sections.title: Latency and cost budgets, co-location, and scaling
sections.summary: The LLM consumes the majority of both latency and cost budgets, followed by TTS, then STT. Engine latency alone is insufficient — network latency between data centers matters. In an optimized system, 75ms of network latency adds ~30% overhead; co-locating all components in the same building drops that to ~5ms. Auto-scaling requires aggressive scale-up but careful scale-down due to stateful long-lived connections. Global deployments matter for user proximity and data residency.

sections.title: Pure speech-to-speech architecture
sections.summary: An emerging alternative to cascading pipelines: a single speech-to-speech model handles function calling and instructions directly (e.g., OpenAI real-time API, Nvidia Voice Chat). Benefits include preserving tone/emotion, full-duplex communication with back-channeling, and better interruption handling. However, these models still struggle with instruction following and tool calling, limiting production use.

sections.title: Q&A: Evals, co-location, guardrails, and thinker-talker pattern
sections.summary: Q&A covers: tool calling evals should target near-100% structure accuracy, with fine-tuning smaller LLMs to improve quality within latency constraints; co-location means running open-source models in the same data center as the orchestrator instead of relying on distant API providers; guardrails and classifiers can be placed before or after the main LLM but add latency pressure, and catching problems before TTS is critical since spoken responses cannot be revoked; the thinker-talker pattern uses a small LLM for conversation flow that issues a single tool call to a larger model for complex requests, keeping the fast path fast.

sections.title: Q&A: Observability and evals for speech-to-speech models
sections.summary: Final Q&A on how observability, logging, and evals change with pure speech-to-speech models. A transcription model can run alongside speech-to-speech to provide auditability of incoming and outgoing audio. Traditional text-to-speech and text-to-text eval concepts no longer apply; evals shift to full-duplex conversation-level metrics covering entire conversations. These evals typically run on top of the base inference API. The talk concludes with thanks to the audience.

Pure speech-to-speech models eliminate traditional text-to-speech and text-to-text eval concepts, requiring new full-duplex conversation-level eval frameworks
